source.title_on_document: AI-assisted design synthesis and human creativity in engineering education

supplement.holds: The text cites Appendix A (photographs of the workshop set-up, p. 4, Section 2.1) and Appendix B (the pre- and post-surveys, p. 5, Section 2.2). Neither is in this 9-page PDF, and the paper does not say whether they form the online supplementary material. The paper does not say that any statistics sit only in the supplement: the U, p, and r values and the arm percentages are printed in Section 3.1 and Figures 1 to 3. Section 2.3 mentions means with standard deviations, which the PDF does not print.

paper_design_summary: Volunteers at a 90-minute engineering workshop (postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, industry mentors) formed their own teams of two to three, and each team drew an envelope that assigned it to ChatGPT-4 with a prompt sheet or to a no-LLM condition with non-LLM web resources allowed, for a 45-minute catapult design-and-build challenge. The Results analyze 7 AI teams and 5 non-AI teams. The paper never gives the number of people. The four team-level creativity measures (designs considered, variety of mechanical principles, uniqueness of the final design, how well the catapult worked) are the participants' own post-survey answers, and individual creative self-efficacy was rated before and after the task.

studies.label: Catapult Challenge workshop (AI-assisted vs non-AI teams)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition, assigned to self-organized teams: each team's representative drew one of 12 shuffled, opaque envelopes (7 marked AI group, 5 marked non-AI group). AI condition: ChatGPT-4 access plus a standardized prompt sheet. Non-AI condition: no large language models; sketching and non-LLM web resources allowed. Team formation itself was not randomized, which is why the authors call the design quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: the session chair prepared 12 shuffled, opaque envelopes (seven designated as “AI group” and five designated as “non-AI group”), and immediately before the task, one representative from each self-organized team drew an envelope to determine random condition assignment.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; also p. 7, Section 4 (“The condition assignment was randomized at the team level”) and p. 8, Section 5

arms.name: AI-assisted teams
arms.description: “AI group”: uninterrupted browser access to ChatGPT-4 (web version 2025-03-13) with a standardized prompt sheet asking for three catapult concepts, each with its mechanical principle, an ASCII sketch, and one improvement tip; teams were free to refine, modify, or disregard the suggestions. 7 teams analyzed (p. 5, Section 3), the same number as the AI envelopes. No count of people is printed.

arms.name: Non-AI (control) teams
arms.description: “non-AI group”: free sketching and permitted use of non-LLM web resources such as Wikipedia or YouTube, with explicit reminders that large language models were prohibited. Whether teams used these resources is not reported. 5 teams analyzed (p. 5, Section 3), the same number as the non-AI envelopes. No count of people is printed.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported; missing values were under 2 percent across all items (p. 5, Section 2.3). The paper never gives the number of people, at assignment or in the analysis. Team counts conflict: volunteers “self-organized into eight teams of two to three members each” (p. 4, Section 2.1), while the Results analyze 12 teams (“AI = 7 teams; non-AI = 5 teams”, p. 5, Section 3), the same number as the envelopes prepared for the draw (12: 7 AI and 5 non-AI, p. 4). At two to three members per team, 12 teams hold at most 36 people and eight teams at most 24 (arithmetic, not printed). The team counts sit in the arm descriptions and in the outcomes' n_units, because the participants fields count people.
participants.who: Convenience cohort of volunteers: postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, and industry mentors; 85 percent engineering background, 62 percent male and 38 percent female, 30 percent under 34 and 70 percent aged 45 or older (as printed). No financial incentives.
participants.country: not_stated (authors at Nazarbayev University, Astana, Kazakhstan; the ethics statement cites the national data protection laws of the Republic of Kazakhstan, p. 8)
participants.quote: A convenience cohort of volunteers, comprising postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, and industry mentors, self-organized into eight teams of two to three members each.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 5, Section 3 (“The sample size is AI = 7 teams; non-AI = 5 teams.”)

ai_tool.how_used: Uninterrupted browser access during the 45-min task, plus a standardized prompt sheet: “Suggest three distinct catapult concepts using only craft sticks, rubber bands, and a spoon. For each concept, list the mechanical principle, a simple ASCII sketch, and one improvement tip.” Teams kept complete autonomy to refine, modify, or disregard ChatGPT's suggestions (p. 4, Section 2.1).

task.description: Team Catapult Challenge adapted from Seelig (2017): design and build a functional tabletop catapult that launches a marble at least 50 cm, from an identical kit (wooden craft sticks, rubber bands, plastic spoons, masking tape, a marble, scissors, a metric measuring tape), with a testing station available.
task.duration: 45-min task inside a 90-min workshop, after a five-minute briefing; pre- and post-surveys about 10 min each

outcomes.name: Quantity (fluency): number of catapult designs the team considered
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item answered by participants right after the task: “How many catapult designs did your team consider?” (5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 design to 5+ designs). Two independent raters transferred the categorical responses to a master coding sheet (κ = 0.94); they did not rate the designs. The paper does not say how members' answers became one value per team. Mann–Whitney U test between arms; the paper calls r an effect size and does not give its formula.

contrasts.reported: Text: non-AI 60% (3 out of 5) considered three or more design variants vs 0% of AI-assisted teams; U = 6, p = 0.073, effect size r = −0.52 (not significant at the paper's α = 0.05; the point estimate favors non-AI teams). Figure 1 (percentage of teams): AI 14.3% 1 design, 85.7% 2 designs, 0.0% each for 3, 4, and 5+ designs; non-AI 0.0% 1 design, 40.0% 2 designs, 40.0% 3 designs, 20.0% 4 designs, 0.0% 5+ designs.

outcomes.name: Variety (flexibility): whether the team's designs used different mechanical principles
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item answered by participants: “Did designs employ different mechanical principles?” (3-point Likert scale: 0 = no variety, 1 = medium variety, 2 = distinct variety). Variety within one team's own designs, so flexibility, not diversity across teams.

contrasts.reported: Text: “40% vs. 29% achieving distinct principles with U = 11.5, p = 0.373, and r = −0.26” (the text does not label the arms; not significant at α = 0.05; the point estimate favors non-AI teams). Figure 2 (left panel): non-AI 40.0% no variety, 20.0% medium variety, 40.0% distinct variety; AI 57.1% no variety, 42.9% medium variety, and no distinct-variety segment, which conflicts with the text's 29%. Figure 4 (p. 7), a radar chart without data labels, places the AI teams' distinct-variety point at the center, marked 0.0.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 6, Figure 2 (left panel); p. 7, Figure 4

outcomes.name: Uniqueness (originality/novelty) of the team's final design
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item answered by participants: “How unique was your final design?” (3-point Likert scale: 0 = standard design, 1 = somewhat unique design, 2 = unique design). The paper calls it “perceived design originality”; the text's “very unique” is the top category, labeled “Unique design” in Figure 2.

contrasts.reported: Text: 40% of non-AI teams rated their final design “very unique” vs 14% (1 out of 7) of AI teams; U = 8.5, p = 0.168, r = −0.40 (not significant at α = 0.05; the point estimate favors non-AI teams). Figure 2 (right panel): non-AI 20.0% standard design, 40.0% somewhat unique design, 40.0% unique design; AI 71.4% standard design, 14.3% somewhat unique design, 14.3% unique design.

outcomes.name: Quality (usefulness): how well the team's final catapult worked
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Post-survey item answered by participants: “How well did your catapult work?” (3-point Likert scale: 0 = failed, 1 = worked somewhat, 2 = worked well). Figure 3 labels the bottom category “Did not work”, and its caption says quality was “assessed by” the teams. Teams had a testing station, but the paper reports the survey answer, not a measured launch distance.

contrasts.reported: Text: all non-AI teams (100%) “worked well” vs 29% (2 out of 7) of AI-assisted teams; U = 5.0, p = 0.051, r = −0.56 (not significant at α = 0.05; the point estimate favors non-AI teams). Figure 3: AI 0.0% did not work, 71.4% worked somewhat, 28.6% worked well; non-AI 0.0% did not work, 0.0% worked somewhat, 100.0% worked well.

outcomes.name: Individual pre- to post-task change in creative self-efficacy, divergent-thinking confidence, problem-solving efficacy, and innovative-thinking self-ratings
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Self-ratings about the person, not the output: a four-item creative self-efficacy scale (three- to five-point Likert) and single-item divergent-thinking confidence, problem-solving efficacy, and innovative-thinking self-ratings adapted from the 4C Creativity Assessment, given in the pre-survey and again in the post-survey (p. 4, Section 2.2). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of pre-to-post change within each condition (p. 5, Section 2.3); no test between arms is reported. AI availability is mixed: the pre-survey came before any AI access, and the paper does not say whether AI access continued during the post-survey. Kept for completeness; not an output-based outcome.

contrasts.reported: Changes “were minimal in both conditions (Wilcoxon |z| < 1.2, p > 0.20 for all comparisons)”. Only these bounds are printed: no exact z or p, no pre or post levels, and no count of people.
Same statement as for the AI-assisted teams: changes “were minimal in both conditions (Wilcoxon |z| < 1.2, p > 0.20 for all comparisons)”. Only these bounds are printed.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met: each self-organized team drew a shuffled, opaque envelope that assigned it to ChatGPT-4 or to no LLM (p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 7, Section 4). The authors call the design quasi-experimental only because teams formed themselves before assignment. Criterion 2 is not met: the paper never states the number of people. It analyzes 7 AI and 5 non-AI teams (p. 5, Section 3) of two to three members each (p. 4), so at most 36 people, or at most 24 if the eight teams stated on p. 4 is right (arithmetic, not printed). Criterion 3 is not met: all four creativity measures are the participants' own post-survey answers about their team's designs (pp. 4 to 5, Section 2.2). The two raters only transcribed the answers, and the authors name reliance on self-reported measures as a limitation (p. 7, Section 4). The paper calls the team measures “objective creativity metrics” (RQ2a, p. 4) and the AI teams' performance “objectively lower” (p. 5, Section 3.2), but Section 2.2 shows that participants answered them in the post-survey, and Section 5 speaks of “relying solely on self-reported measures” (p. 8). The paper belongs in the screening report as a small randomized experiment whose only outcomes are self-reported.

one_line_finding: With 7 ChatGPT-4 teams and 5 no-LLM teams analyzed, the AI teams' own post-survey answers were lower on all four dimensions, and no difference was significant at 0.05: designs considered (U = 6, p = 0.073), variety (U = 11.5, p = 0.373), uniqueness (U = 8.5, p = 0.168), and catapult worked well (29% vs 100%, U = 5.0, p = 0.051) (p. 5, Section 3.1; Figures 1 to 3, p. 6).
open_questions: Number of teams: p. 4 says volunteers formed “eight teams of two to three members each”, while the envelope procedure (12 envelopes, 7 AI and 5 non-AI, p. 4) and the Results (“AI = 7 teams; non-AI = 5 teams”, p. 5, Section 3) give 12 teams. The printed U, p, and r values fit 7 and 5 teams (see notes). The number of people is never stated.

Variety: the text gives “40% vs. 29% achieving distinct principles” (p. 5), but Figure 2 shows no AI team with distinct variety (57.1% none, 42.9% medium, p. 6), and Figure 4 places the AI teams at 0 on that axis (p. 7). The printed U = 11.5 fits the figures, not the text (see notes).

Section 3.1 says “Uniqueness approaching significance” and the other three “showing a trend”, but uniqueness has the second-largest p (0.168); quality (0.051) and quantity (0.073) have the smallest (p. 5).
Section 3.2 says non-AI teams “significantly outperformed” AI teams, which contradicts Section 3.1's statement that no difference is significant at α = 0.05 (p. 5).
The paper does not say whether each team-level item was answered once per team or by every member, or how members' answers became one team value; the tests use one value per team (7 vs 5).
Whether the Quality answer reflects the testing-station result or only the team's own judgment; the paper presents it as a post-survey item that the teams assessed.
Section 2.3 says descriptive statistics included means with standard deviations, but none are printed; the document does not say whether the supplement holds them.

Section 2.1 says the blind envelope draw provided “baseline equivalence across these variables” (p. 4), and Section 4 says “baseline equivalence was examined” (p. 7), but no baseline comparison is reported.
Whether control teams used the permitted non-LLM web resources, and whether AI teams could use them too. This decides between ai_vs_active (coded) and ai_vs_bau.
notes: Design class lab_rct: conditions were assigned by random envelope draw at the team level in a supervised 90-min workshop. The authors call the study quasi-experimental because teams self-organized before assignment, and they decline a causal interpretation (p. 7, Section 4; p. 8, Section 5). Participant counts stay null because the paper prints no count of people; the team counts (7 AI, 5 non-AI) sit in the arm descriptions and in n_units. All four team-level creativity outcomes are the participants' own post-survey answers, so measure is self_report and scored_on_output is false; the two raters only transcribed the answers (κ = 0.94, p. 5). Directions are no_clear_difference because the paper reports no difference as significant at α = 0.05, although every point estimate favors the non-AI teams (p. 5, Section 3.1). Reconciler's check, arithmetic and not printed: with 7 AI and 5 non-AI teams, the category percentages in Figures 1 to 3 reproduce the printed U values (6, 11.5, 8.5, 5.0). A normal approximation with continuity correction and no tie correction gives p = 0.074, 0.372, 0.167, and 0.051 against the printed 0.073, 0.373, 0.168, and 0.051 (largest gap 0.0013), and z divided by the square root of 12 reproduces the printed |r| (0.52, 0.26, 0.40, 0.56). For Variety, 2 of 7 AI teams with distinct principles (the text's 29%) would give U between 13 and 17.5, depending on how the other five AI teams split between no and medium variety (14.5 with four at no variety, as in Figure 2), never the printed 11.5. The printed test therefore matches Figures 2 and 4, not the text. S1-O5 (individual pre/post self-perceptions) is kept with question none; it concerns the person, not the output. Comparison type ai_vs_active because the control arm was permitted named non-LLM web resources (as in reconciled c010, Study 2). It could also be read as ai_vs_bau: web use was permitted, not required, its use is not reported, and Section 3.3 describes non-AI teams as “working without external input” (p. 7). Demographics are recorded as printed: 30 percent under 34 and 70 percent aged 45 or older sum to 100 percent and leave no one aged 34 to 44. Data availability: raw data “will be made available by the authors without undue reservation” (p. 8); no URL. Ethics approval obtained 18 October 2024 (p. 8). Final check, 2026-10-05: no challenge file exists for c121. The challenges folder holds none, the pipeline status lists no challenges for this paper, and the finishing run of 2026-10-05 ran checkers only for c075, c109, and c126 (RESUME.md). No checker problem was resolved, so final.challenge_resolution is empty and its three counts are zero. The finalizer checked the form against the PDF instead (pp. 1 to 9, page images and text layer). Every quote in the form appears on its cited page, including those in the reconciliation object. “Did not work” and the “Unique design” legend are figure labels and appear only in the page image (p. 6). Every number in the reported strings matches Section 3.1 (p. 5) and the data labels of Figures 1 to 3 (p. 6). The reconciler's U, p, and r arithmetic holds after two corrections above: the p-value gap reaches 0.0013, not 0.001, and the Variety alternative is a range. New from the source: Figure 4 (p. 7) places the AI teams at 0 on the distinct-variety axis, which agrees with Figure 2 and not with the text's 29% (added to S1-O2 and open question 2). Section 2.1 says the blind draw provided baseline equivalence (added to open question 8). eligibility.reason now answers the paper's word “objective” for the team measures (RQ2a, p. 4; Section 3.2, p. 5). Spec alignment: paper_design_summary, both arm descriptions, participants.exclusions, eligibility.reason, and one_line_finding now say 'analyzed' for the 7 and 5 teams in the Results. source.supplement was already filled, and the reanalysis rule does not apply. The reconciliation object lists no unresolved difference. Eligibility is unchanged: criterion 1 met, criteria 2 and 3 not met, core no.

reconciliation.notes: This file replaces an earlier reconciled c121.json. That version compared an earlier pair of raw forms whose values differ from the current c121.A.json and c121.B.json, so every difference above was rebuilt from the current forms and checked again against the markdown and the PDF pages (pp. 1 to 9). Choices that also appeared in the earlier version (null people counts, no_clear_difference directions, figure_only, S1-O5 with two within-condition contrasts) were derived again from the source and the house conventions, not copied.

open_items.item: Number of teams and of people (open question 1). Section 2.1 says eight teams, while the 12 envelopes (p. 4) and the Results (p. 5) give 12 teams, 7 AI and 5 non-AI. No count of people is printed. Criterion 2 fails under either team count: teams of two to three members hold at most 36 people (12 teams) or 24 (eight teams). The raw data are with the authors, who the paper says will make them available (p. 8).

Variety, text against figures (open question 2). The text gives 29% of AI teams with distinct principles (p. 5), but Figures 2 and 4 show none (pp. 6 to 7), and the printed U = 11.5 fits the figures. The answer changes only the S1-O2 record: the outcome is a self-report, and criterion 2 fails.

Section 3.1 says “Uniqueness approaching significance” although its p (0.168) is the second largest of the four (open question 3). The form codes each direction from the printed U and p, so the wording changes no code.

Section 3.2 says non-AI teams “significantly outperformed” AI teams, against Section 3.1, which finds no difference significant at α = 0.05 (open question 4). The form follows the printed tests (no_clear_difference), so no code depends on the wording.

How the members' answers became one value per team (open question 5). The tests use one value per team (7 against 5). Appendix B, which holds the surveys and is not in this PDF, may show whether each team answered once. The rule for combining answers needs the authors. Criterion 3 fails however the answers were combined, because they are self-reports.

Whether the Quality answer reflects the testing-station result or only the team's own judgment (open question 6). The paper reports only the post-survey answer, which the Figure 3 caption says the teams assessed (p. 6). The reported outcome is a self-report under either reading, and criterion 2 fails regardless.

Means with standard deviations (open question 7). Section 2.3 says the descriptive statistics included them (p. 5), but none are printed, and the paper does not say whether the online supplement holds them. They matter for extraction only.

Baseline equivalence (open question 8). Section 2.1 says the blind draw provided it (p. 4), and Section 4 says it was examined (p. 7), but no comparison is printed. Criterion 1 rests on the envelope draw, which the paper states (p. 4).

Comparison type (open question 9). Whether control teams used the permitted non-LLM web resources, and whether AI teams could use them too, decides between ai_vs_active (coded) and ai_vs_bau. Eligibility does not depend on it.
